newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy government gets go-ahead for mini-budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy government gets go-ahead for mini-budget.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi got support from coalition partners on Wednesday for a corrective budget to put Italy back on track for European economic and monetary union (EMU), party leaders said.
The mini-budget is expected to include around 16 trillion lire ($9.5 billion) of deficit-cutting measures and will almost certainly be approved by the cabinet on Thursday.

"There was broad backing for the government on its global aims...although there is some fine tuning to be done," said Franco Marini, head of the Popular Party, following a meeting of coalition leaders and cabinet ministers.
Fausto Bertinotti, head of the hardleft Communist Refoundation, told reporters that he had won his battle to prevent any further tax hikes or cuts to social spending.
"The meeting went well," he said. "There will be no new taxes and no reduction in welfare spending."

Centre-right parties had called on Prodi to embark on an overhaul of the welfare state with the mini-budget, arguing that structural spending changes were the only way to ensure that Italy was ready for the launch of the single European currency.

A corrective budget was needed after data from the first quarter indicated that Italy's deficit this year was heading towards 3.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) against three percent demanded by the Maastricht Treaty.

Refoundation, which holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament, had threatened to bring Prodi down if he touched social spending. Bertinotti indicated that with the budget out of the way, he was now willing to discuss reform.
"This opens a chapter which will be decisive - the reform of the welfare state. It is a chapter that is wide open," he said.

The mini-budget will raise a third of the cash needed by getting firms to cough up taxes on their huge severance payment funds ahead of schedule and by holding back end-of-contract retirement settlements to state workers for six months.

A further third will come from a reduction in spending by certain state funds while the rest of the money would be raised from fiscal measures such as new methods of collecting inheritance tax, Bertinotti said.
The Italian lira strengthened when the coalition reached a deal, but analysts said the budget did not look strong.
"There are no structural cuts on the spending side," Giovanni Mossetti, chief economist at Milan brokers Caboto, told Reuters Financial Television.
"Not only are these one-off measures, these are one-off measures that will come back with a vengeance next year...they are trying to sweep the problem under the carpet," she added.
Big Italian industry will also be disappointed about the budget, especially the advanced taxes on the severance funds.

Firms regularly dip into the savings, held over for employees when they retire, as a cheap source of self-financing and have warned that any raids on these resources would harm trade at a weak moment in the business cycle.

Statistics office Istat said on Wednesday that the jobless rate rose to 12.4 percent of the workforce in January from 12.2 percent last October, while employers' body Confindustria said industrial output fell 2.9 percent year-on-year in March.
But after years of budgetary rigour, the government's options for swift belt tightening were limited.

The Green Party leader in the upper house of parliament, Maurizio Pieroni, told reporters after the coalition meeting that "a collective sacrifice" was called for if Italy was to make the grade for the single European currency.
